newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sydkraft board to discuss reactor closures.
newsitem.headline: Sydkraft board to discuss reactor closures.

text.p: Swedish power company Sydkraft said its board would meet on Friday this week to discuss how the company would handle the proposed closure of its two nuclear reactors at Barseback at the southern tip of Sweden.
The closures, to proceed by July 1998 and July 2001, are laid down in an energy agreement approved by Sweden's ruling Social Democrats and two other political parties this week.

A company spokesman said the company was demanding full compensation from the government for closing the reactors which could cost the state up to 20 billion crowns ($2.7 billion), according to company estimates.
"We want the compensation in the form of electricity. Megawatt for megawatt," the spokesman told Reuters.
But Industry and Trade Minister Anders Sundstrom said the cost for a closure would be lower.
"This 20 billion crowns is pure invention," Sundstrom told journalists after Wednesday's energy debate in parliament. "These are old plants whose book value is much lower than that."
Sundstrom did not want to disclose how much he thought Barseback was worth but said he was convinced the government would be able to reach agreement with Sydkraft.
Sydkraft's spokesman said there were various options open to the company, Sweden's largest independent power supplier.
Sydkraft could try to take the issue to the European Commission to block the agreement that was approved this week by the ruling Social Democrats, the Centre and Left parties.
The agreement lays down the procedure for phasing out Sweden's nuclear power industry.
But Swedish business daily Dagens Industri said the owners of Sydkraft were split on how to proceed.
Dagens Industri said the five community councils that owned 37.9 percent of votes in Sydkraft did not want to fight against the agreement that was reached by a parliamentary majority.
But the paper said the majority of Sydkraft's owners did not want to accept the move to close the first reactor as soon as 1998, before the September general election.
Germany's Preussen Elektra and Statkraft hold 49.3 percent of votes in Sydkraft.
The government said late Tuesday that negotiations would be started with Sydkraft over closing its reactors at Barseback.
"We have not heard from them," the company spokesman said.

The government said in a statement the state-controlled power company, Vattenfall, would be actively involved in the changes in the energy system, helping to compensate Sydkraft for its loss of electricity.
A law on decommissioning nuclear power plants would be passed.

The agreement was also designed to develop an ecologically sustainable energy supply system. This included stimulating new electricity production from renewable energy sources and promoting energy conservation.
"The energy policy programme will give rise to state expenditure of nine billion crowns over a seven year period," the Industry and Trade Ministry said in a statement.
"The programme will receive full funding. The parties behind the agreement will together decide on suitable methods of financing."
-- Belinda Goldsmith, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1045 ($ = 7.362 Swedish Crowns)
